title: How do you change a schema on a large production table without downtime using the expand-and-contract pattern (add nullable column → dual-write from the app → backfill in batches → switch reads/add constraints → drop the old column later), and why is a single `ALTER TABLE ... NOT NULL DEFAULT` on a huge table dangerous (table rewrite + long lock)?
shortTitle: Zero-Downtime Schema Change on a Large Table — Expand-and-Contract
topicTitle: How do you change a schema on a large production table without downtime using th

s1_definition.profdef: Expand-and-contract (also called parallel change) performs a schema change on a large table in small, backward-compatible steps so the application stays online throughout. You expand by adding the new structure as nullable and non-breaking, dual-write to both old and new from the application, backfill historical rows in small batches, switch reads and add constraints once the new column is fully populated, and finally contract by dropping the old column after all code uses the new one. A single blocking `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT ...` on a huge table can be dangerous because on some databases it forces a full table rewrite while holding a lock, freezing the table for the duration.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to renovate the main vault while it is still serving customers all day. You cannot shut the vault for a week. So you build the new section alongside the old (expand), keep recording every deposit in both the old and new ledgers for a while (dual-write), slowly copy the historical records over in small nightly batches (backfill), then once everything matches, start trusting the new ledger and stop using the old (switch), and only much later tear down the old section (contract). Doing it in one giant locked operation would be like bolting the vault shut mid-day.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand (add nullable), dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads and add constraints, then contract (drop old) — never one blocking ALTER that rewrites and locks a huge table.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Expand-and-contract (also called parallel change) performs a schema change on a large table in small, backward-compatible steps so the application stays online throughout. You expand by adding the new structure as nullable and non-breaking, dual-write to both old and new from the application, backfill historical rows in small batches, switch reads and add constraints once the new column is fully populated, and finally contract by dropping the old column after all code uses the new one. A single blocking `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT ...` on a huge table can be dangerous because on some databases it forces a full table rewrite while holding a lock, freezing the table for the duration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to renovate the main vault while it is still serving customers all day. You cannot shut the vault for a week. So you build the new section alongside the old (expand), keep recording every deposit in both the old and new ledgers for a while (dual-write), slowly copy the historical records over in small nightly batches (backfill), then once everything matches, start trusting the new ledger and stop using the old (switch), and only much later tear down the old section (contract). Doing it in one giant locked operation would be like bolting the vault shut mid-day.

**One line to remember:** Expand (add nullable), dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads and add constraints, then contract (drop old) — never one blocking ALTER that rewrites and locks a huge table.

sections.s2_technical:
The danger of the naive approach comes first. On many databases, `ALTER TABLE big ADD COLUMN x TYPE NOT NULL DEFAULT val` historically rewrites every row to store the default and holds an exclusive lock on the table while it does so. On a table with hundreds of millions of rows that can take many minutes or hours, during which no reads or writes proceed — effectively an outage. Similar hazards exist for changing a column type, adding a `NOT NULL` constraint that must validate every existing row, or adding a foreign key that scans the whole table. (Modern PostgreSQL optimizes adding a column with a constant default to avoid the rewrite, but type changes, non-constant defaults, and constraint validation still lock or scan, so you cannot rely on it generally.) The core principle is: avoid any single DDL that takes a long lock or rewrites the whole table while the application is live.

Expand-and-contract breaks the change into safe steps where each step is individually fast and backward compatible, so old and new code and old and new data coexist. Say you are renaming/retyping a column, for example splitting a `full_name` into `first_name`/`last_name`, or changing `amount` from integer paise to a decimal.

Step 1, Expand: add the new column as nullable with no heavy default. `ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN amount_decimal NUMERIC(15,2) NULL`. Adding a nullable column with no default is a fast metadata-only change on most databases — no rewrite, minimal lock.

Step 2, Dual-write: deploy application code that writes to both the old and the new column on every insert and update. Now every new or modified row has the new column populated correctly, while old rows still have it null. The app still reads from the old column, so behavior is unchanged.

Step 3, Backfill: populate the new column for historical rows in small batches, for example a few thousand rows per transaction in a loop, with a short pause between batches. Batching avoids one giant transaction that locks the table or bloats the WAL; it keeps each transaction short so it does not block live traffic. You run this as a background job until no rows remain with a null new column.

Step 4, Switch and constrain: once every row has the new column populated, deploy code that reads from the new column. Then you can safely add constraints — make it `NOT NULL` (ideally using a two-phase approach: add a `NOT VALID` check constraint, validate it without a full lock, then set NOT NULL), add indexes (concurrently), and so on. Reads now come from the new column.

Step 5, Contract: after a safe period during which the new column is proven in production and no code references the old one, drop the old column. `ALTER TABLE accounts DROP COLUMN amount_old`. Dropping is fast metadata-wise, and you do it last so you always have a rollback path until then.

The senior points: every step is reversible up to the contract, so if something goes wrong you roll back the deploy, not the data. The dual-write window is what makes it safe — both representations are valid simultaneously. You use versioned migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) for each step so they are ordered, auditable, and repeatable across environments. For the backfill you throttle to protect replication lag and I/O. And you never couple a long-running DDL with a schema-change deploy; you keep locks short and let the batched background job do the heavy lifting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India stores `balance` as an integer number of paise in a 400-million-row `accounts` table, and the team needs it as a `DECIMAL(15,2)` rupees column for a new reporting system. A junior proposed `ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN balance_decimal NUMERIC(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, which on their database would rewrite all 400 million rows under an exclusive lock — a multi-hour outage during business hours. The DBA mandated the expand-and-contract pattern instead so the bank stays online.

Our mini-project simulates the pattern: a `MigrationRunner` that adds the nullable column, a `DualWriteAccountService` that writes both representations, a `Backfiller` that fills historical rows in small batches, and a `Demo` that walks through expand, dual-write, backfill, switch, and contract.

The code will contain: an `AccountRow` with both old and new balance fields, a `TableSim` acting as the large table, a `Backfiller.backfillInBatches()`, a `DualWriteAccountService`, and a `Demo` tracing the full pattern.

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -cp target/expand-contract-migration-1.0.0.jar com.bank.migrate.MigrationApplication

# Expected:
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a simulated 1000-row accounts table (standing in for 400 million), each with a `balancePaise` and a null `balanceDecimal`.

Step 1 (Expand): the nullable `balanceDecimal` column exists but is null for every row. Adding it was a fast metadata-only operation with no table rewrite and no long lock, so the application never paused. All 1000 rows show a null decimal.

Step 2 (Dual-write): the application now writes both columns on every change. When row 1's balance is updated to 55000 paise, the service also sets its decimal to 550.00. New and updated rows self-heal to the correct new value while the app still reads the old column, so behavior is unchanged.

Step 3 (Backfill): a background job fills the historical rows in batches of 100, each batch a short transaction with a throttle pause between them. This avoids one giant locking transaction and protects replication lag. After it completes, zero rows have a null decimal.

Step 4 (Switch and constrain): with every row populated, the application is deployed to read from the new column, and the `NOT NULL` constraint is added safely using the add-NOT-VALID-then-validate approach so there is no long exclusive lock.

Step 5 (Contract): after a bake period proving the new column in production, the old `balancePaise` column is dropped. The demo stops here, noting the switch and drop, having kept the bank online the entire time.

```
After expand, null decimal rows = 1000
Row 1 after dual-write: decimal=550.00
Oct 25, 2026 17:03:00 INFO: Backfilled up to row 100
... (batches) ...
Oct 25, 2026 17:03:00 INFO: Backfilled up to row 1000
After backfill, null decimal rows = 0
Ready to switch reads to balance_decimal, then drop balance_paise.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  LARGE accounts table (400M rows), app stays ONLINE throughout
    │
    ▼  Step 1 EXPAND: ADD COLUMN balance_decimal NULL   (fast, metadata-only)
    │
    ▼  Step 2 DUAL-WRITE: app writes paise AND decimal   (new rows correct)
    │
    ▼  Step 3 BACKFILL: small batches + throttle         (short txns, no big lock)
    │     [100][100]...[100]  until 0 null rows
    │
    ▼  Step 4 SWITCH reads → decimal ; add NOT NULL via NOT VALID→VALIDATE
    │
    ▼  Step 5 CONTRACT: DROP COLUMN balance_paise         (last, reversible until here)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  vs DANGEROUS: ALTER ... NOT NULL DEFAULT → full rewrite + exclusive lock → OUTAGE
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Zero-Downtime Migration ═══

  ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ CI/CD    │─────→│ Flyway migrations     │  V2 expand → V4 constrain → V5 contract
  └──────────┘      └──────────┬───────────┘
                               │ each step small + ordered
                               ▼
  ┌────────────┐  dual-write   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ App (×N)   │──────────────→│ PostgreSQL primary     │
  │ old+new    │               │ accounts (400M rows)   │
  └────────────┘               └──────────┬────────────┘
                                          │ WAL replication (watch lag)
                                          ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────┐
                               │ Backfill batch job    │ throttled, resumable
                               └──────────────────────┘
```

Each migration step is a small ordered Flyway script; the app dual-writes; a throttled batch job backfills while watching replication lag.
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Expand-and-Contract ═══

  ┌─ Step invariants (each reversible until contract) ───────┐
  │ Expand:    add NULLABLE col, no heavy default (fast)      │
  │ Dual-write: old+new both valid simultaneously             │
  │ Backfill:  small batches, short txns, throttle            │
  │ Constrain: NOT VALID → VALIDATE → SET NOT NULL            │
  │ Contract:  drop old LAST                                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ DualWriteAccountService  │──▶│ AccountRow   │
  │ + updateBalance()        │   │ paise+decimal│
  └──────────────────────────┘   └──────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────┐──────────▲ fills
  │ Backfiller               │  reads
  │ + backfillInBatches()    │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. expand (nullable column)
  2. dual-write live traffic
  3. backfillInBatches(100) until 0 null
  4. switch reads + add NOT NULL safely
  5. drop old column (contract)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To change the schema of a large production table without downtime I use the expand-and-contract pattern, breaking the change into small backward-compatible steps so old and new data and code coexist and the application stays online. First I expand by adding the new column as nullable with no heavy default, which is a fast metadata-only change. Then I dual-write from the application, so every new or updated row populates both the old and the new column while reads still come from the old one. Then I backfill the historical rows in small throttled batches rather than one giant transaction, keeping each transaction short so it never takes a long lock and so replication does not fall behind. Once every row is populated I switch reads to the new column and add constraints safely — for NOT NULL I add a NOT VALID check, validate it without an exclusive lock, then set NOT NULL, and I build indexes concurrently. Finally, after a bake period, I contract by dropping the old column last, so I always have a rollback path until that point.

The reason I avoid a single `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT` on a huge table is that on many databases it rewrites every row to store the default while holding an exclusive lock, which on a 400-million-row table is a multi-hour outage. In our National Bank of India system we needed to change the account balance from integer paise to a decimal rupees column on exactly such a table, and a one-shot ALTER would have frozen the vault during business hours, so the DBA mandated expand-and-contract and we stayed fully online. The senior points I add are that every step before the contract is reversible so I roll back a deploy rather than data, that I drive each step through versioned Flyway or Liquibase migrations so they are ordered and auditable, and that I throttle the backfill to protect replication lag and I/O. The line I remember is: expand with a nullable column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads and constrain safely, then contract by dropping the old column — never one blocking ALTER that rewrites and locks the whole table.
